opus-5.5.text:
That paper is one I'm really proud of, and it's mostly Alex's work. Michael and I were along for the ride.

The question we kept getting about the lottery ticket work was: "This is a neat scientific curiosity, but does it matter for people who actually want to prune networks?" The standard pruning recipe was to train the network, prune the lowest-magnitude weights, and then fine-tune the remaining weights at a small learning rate for a while to recover accuracy. Rewinding is a different idea. You take the pruned network, reset the surviving weights to their values from early in training, and then retrain from there with the original schedule.

Alex compared these head to head and found that rewinding consistently matched or beat fine-tuning. He then simplified it further with what we called learning rate rewinding. Instead of resetting the weights, you keep the trained weights but replay the original learning rate schedule from that earlier point. That turned out to work as well as or better than weight rewinding in many settings.

The really striking result was that this simple procedure was competitive with much more complicated, state-of-the-art pruning methods, all of which had their own bells and whistles. Iterative magnitude pruning with rewinding is about as simple as you can get, and it held its own.

So for me, the paper revealed two things:

- **The lottery ticket ideas aren't just a curiosity.** The procedure that came out of trying to understand why sparse networks can train turns out to be a genuinely strong practical pruning algorithm.
- **What matters most may be the retraining, not the pruning criterion.** A lot of the field's attention had gone into clever ways to decide which weights to remove. This work suggests that how you retrain afterward, especially giving the network a real stretch of high-learning-rate training again, matters at least as much. Fine-tuning at a tiny learning rate was leaving a lot on the table.

I'd also be honest about the limits. This doesn't make pruning cheap, because you still train the full network first, sometimes several times if you prune iteratively. The dream of finding these subnetworks at the start of training and saving all that compute is still mostly unrealized. But as a bridge between "here's a scientific phenomenon" and "here's something a practitioner should actually use," I think that paper did what we hoped it would.

r001.rationale: The response says lottery-ticket ideas became a practical pruning algorithm, but does not state that sparse networks found early in training are roughly competitive with networks produced by traditional end-of-training pruning.

r002.rationale: It contrasts weight resetting with keeping trained weights and replaying the learning-rate schedule, explaining that schedule replay worked as well as or better than weight rewinding. This identifies schedule restarting as an alternative explanation for the benefit.

r003.rationale: It says learning-rate rewinding, which keeps trained weights and replays the schedule, worked as well as or better than weight rewinding in many settings.

r004.rationale: It says that after pruning, giving the network a substantial stretch of high-learning-rate training again matters, and that fine-tuning at a tiny learning rate leaves performance on the table.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think that paper is actually one of my favorite things to come out of the lottery ticket line of work, and I say that partly because it's Alex's paper and he deserves the credit for it, but also because it takes the lottery ticket idea and asks the question I think everybody should have been asking, which is: does any of this matter for pruning in practice?

So just to set it up a little bit. The standard way you prune a network is you train it to completion, you remove some of the weights, and then you fine-tune. You keep the weights where they are and you train for a little while longer at a small learning rate to recover whatever accuracy you lost. That's the recipe people have used for decades. What the lottery ticket work does instead is, after you prune, you rewind the weights back to their values from very early in training, or from initialization, and you retrain from there, with the original learning rate schedule. And the interesting thing we'd found was that this rewinding approach could get you to much sparser networks than fine-tuning would, at least in the settings where it worked.

What Alex did was take that comparison seriously and run it across the board. Image classification, ResNets on ImageNet, machine translation with transformers, a bunch of different sparsities. And the headline result is that rewinding, either rewinding the weights or even just rewinding the learning rate schedule while keeping the trained weights, consistently matches or beats fine-tuning. Often by a meaningful margin at high sparsity. And the learning rate rewinding result is kind of the surprising one, because it says that a lot of what matters isn't the specific early weights, it's that you give the network a chance to retrain with a real learning rate rather than this tiny one that fine-tuning uses.

So what does it reveal? I'd say a couple of things. First, it says the lottery ticket phenomenon isn't just a curiosity about initialization. It actually has a practical payload. If you care about getting the sparsest possible network at a given accuracy, you should probably be rewinding instead of fine-tuning, and that's a concrete, actionable thing that came out of what was originally a very scientific, "why do networks train" kind of question.

Second, and I think this is the more honest reading, it slightly complicates the story we were telling about lottery tickets. If learning rate rewinding does nearly as well as weight rewinding, then the special thing about the early weights is less special than the original paper might have suggested. The structure you find by pruning is important, and the training procedure you use afterward is important, but the specific initial values might be a smaller part of the picture than we thought. I'm fine with that. I'd rather have the phenomenon explained than have it stay mysterious.

And the third thing, which I'd flag as a caveat, is that this is all about accuracy at a given sparsity. It doesn't say anything about whether you can find these networks cheaply. You still have to train the full dense network first and prune afterward, so from the standpoint of saving compute during training, which is the thing everyone really wants, we're not there. That's still the open problem.

r002.rationale: It notes that learning-rate rewinding nearly matches weight rewinding and says the specific early weights may matter less than retraining with a real learning rate.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts the importance of a real learning rate with the specific early weights, communicating that learning-rate restarting mattered more in these experiments.

r004.rationale: It recommends rewinding instead of fine-tuning and explains that retraining with a real learning rate can recover accuracy, unlike fine-tuning's tiny rate.

astra-6.text:
I think Alex’s work showed that one of the most useful ideas to come out of the lottery ticket work was rewinding itself. You don’t necessarily have to be interested in finding a winning ticket at initialization for that idea to improve pruning.

The traditional recipe is to train a network, prune it, and then fine-tune it at a small learning rate. What Alex explored was whether you could do better by going back and replaying part of the training process. You can rewind the weights to an earlier point, as we did in the lottery ticket work, or keep the trained weights and rewind just the learning-rate schedule. And that latter approach turns out to be really effective.

That’s an interesting distinction because learning-rate rewinding isn’t really a claim about a special initialization. It’s a claim about how you should train a network after you’ve pruned it. So I see the paper as taking an idea motivated by lottery tickets and showing that it has a much broader practical use. It also raises the bar for comparisons: if you’re proposing a new pruning method, you need to distinguish the benefit of your pruning rule from the benefit of giving the pruned network a better training schedule.

r001.rationale: The response discusses rewinding and traditional pruning but does not say sparse networks found early in training are roughly competitive with networks pruned at the end.

r002.rationale: It explains that learning-rate rewinding is effective and says comparisons must separate the pruning rule’s benefit from the benefit of a better training schedule, identifying schedule changes as an alternative explanation for rewinding’s gains.

r003.rationale: The response calls learning-rate rewinding effective but does not state that it mattered more than rewinding weights in Alex’s experiments.

r004.rationale: It describes replaying a learning-rate schedule after pruning, but does not recommend returning to a higher learning rate to help the pruned network recover.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Alex’s paper makes a really nice connection between the lottery ticket work and pruning as people actually practice it. In the lottery ticket experiments, we were taking a pruned network and rewinding it to an earlier point in training. In conventional pruning, you generally keep the trained weights and fine-tune them, often with a small learning rate.

What Alex showed is that a lot of the benefit comes from revisiting the learning-rate schedule. You can keep the weights you have after pruning, rewind the learning rate, and train again using that earlier part of the schedule. That works remarkably well—often as well as or better than rewinding the weights too—and improves on the usual fine-tuning approach.

So I wouldn’t interpret that as saying that finding the original initialization is essential to practical pruning. It’s more that the lottery ticket perspective led us to question how we retrain a network after pruning. The weights matter, but giving the pruned network a meaningful opportunity to learn again matters enormously. That’s a useful practical lesson, even if your goal has nothing to do with finding a winning ticket.

r002.rationale: It identifies revisiting the learning-rate schedule as a major source of benefit and says this works while keeping the post-pruning weights, separating the schedule effect from resetting weights.

r003.rationale: It says schedule-based retraining works often as well as or better than also rewinding the weights, communicating that the schedule mattered more in these experiments.

r004.rationale: It contrasts small-learning-rate fine-tuning with rewinding to an earlier part of the schedule after pruning and training again, conveying a return to a higher learning rate to help the network recover.
